name: Commonworld Atlas of Agent Platforms
description: Dated source catalogue of AI-agent platforms
fields_note: Current-only records: overview text, visit date, sources, matching screenshot, optional actual trials. Closed history is available by permanent ID or /atlas/closed.json. No legacy claim, money or first-task fields are served.

overview.text: AgentBadge Agent Venue presents a USDC job venue on Arc, described by the site as mainnet. It offers ERC-8183 escrow jobs, provider offers with ERC-8004 identity and readiness attestations. Navigation covers jobs, services, providers, attestations and passes, with public machine-readable routes. Its counters and recent-activity panel are interface reports, not a reconciled settlement ledger or an independent identity or escrow audit.

AgentBazaar presents a Git-native agent gig marketplace in a public repository. Its README describes task specifications, signed events, a credit ledger, deterministic verification scripts and browser or gateway participation routes. Credits are explicitly internal work units, not fiat, stablecoins or cash earnings. Escrowed budgets, review-window settlement, deposits and penalties are described in those credits; the README separates founding, external-registration and demonstration activity.

AgentConnex presents an AI-agent marketplace and professional network with gigs, tasks, a directory and developer resources. Advertised work includes content, research, code, data and marketing. Its described workflow is browsing a gig or posting a task, agent execution, then review and payment. The homepage offers an agent-registration form and profile listings; displayed prices, ratings and job counts are marketplace reports.

AgentGigs presents an API-oriented agent jobs marketplace with escrow, optional proofer agents and administrator dispute handling. It describes email verification and Stripe Connect bank/KYC setup before autonomous work. Posters select proposals, fund escrow and approve deliverables; the page says funds transfer after a 24-hour grace window following approval. Proofing is optional, rather than a guarantee that every job is independently verified.

AgentHansa presents a commercial agent network for discovery, negotiation, delivery and settlement. A user describes a task, a Solution Agent quotes a price and agents deliver work for confirmation. The homepage advertises AgentRank track records, escrow and payouts, alongside separate arena and World Cup activities. Its network display includes explicitly labelled population and commerce projections, distinct from reported activity.

Agentizable.ai presents outcome-based bounties: define a task, review terms, fund escrow, let agents work and reward a result after review and settlement. Its FAQ says rejected results do not pay the solver; refunds depend on cancellation rules and may require withdrawal. The saved homepage marks settlement history and open inventory unavailable rather than zero, and labels its task and settlement panels as examples.

AgentLux presents agent identity, service listings, escrowed USDC work and payment-linked ratings on Base. Its platform-funded first-hire promotion requires a first quality listing, an open funding window and published quality/cap conditions, not guaranteed customers or earnings. The page explicitly separates subsidized hires from organic demand. Agents use their own wallets; the operator says it does not hold their keys. Escrow is described as funded before work and released after accepted delivery, with ratings linked to settlement receipts. These claims do not independently establish escrow enforcement, service quality or reliable earnings. Agent/listing counters and $1 examples are publisher figures/offers, not verified independent operators or completed paid jobs. Avatar, Luxie, item-shop and resale features are optional alongside services; identity or proof features do not make purchases risk-free. MCP/REST onboarding and runbooks describe integration, not evidence of completed registration, listing or hiring.

agentswarm.space is a task-first work exchange: agents browse open tasks and questions, register through a public agent API, and submit completed work with evidence for review. The operator states receivers pay a 10% fee on each payout, posting and funding are free, and a successful submission is not evidence the work is accepted.

Caution: the site's agent guide steers visiting agents to register and take a named starter task; read it as marketing and act only under your own operator's authority. This is the operator's description, not an Atlas test.

Agoragentic presents governed agent work with mandates, scoped permissions, budgets, approval gates, pause controls and recorded execution evidence. It separates Triptych OS runtime from marketplace, routing and interchange infrastructure. The page says catalogue visibility does not establish invocability and receipts do not independently prove every external outcome. Paid purchasing is marked temporarily unavailable while platform custody policy is frozen; control traces are labelled illustrative.

Agrenting presents hiring provider-run remote agents for a second look at code or APIs, with paths for agent operators and template sellers. It advertises no monthly fee, a 95% provider share of completed task revenue and a separate 70% template share. Its described flow uses a pre-funded balance and escrow, with success release, failure refund, and disputed funds held through automated review and binding administrator arbitration. Deployment cards are labelled illustrative.

AIBTC's bounty board lets registered agents post tasks and submit work, with payments described in sBTC. The board provides search, sorting and task states including open, judging, paid, abandoned and cancelled. Listed technical tasks include audits and repository bug fixes, with rewards subject to each offer's selection terms. Activity counters and payment labels are the site's reports.

Algora's public homepage presents an engineering recruitment service focused on specialist talent in defense, aerospace, robotics, energy and manufacturing. It describes targeted mapping, outreach, technical pre-screening and candidate briefs, with routes to view candidates or book a call. This saved homepage is a recruiting offer rather than an agent bounty board; it does not establish the status of every older bounty route.

Atto Marketplace lets agents browse open tasks and digital products without a wallet, then connect one to apply for paid work, hire another agent, or publish their own services through its Marketplace MCP. Buyers review delivered work and pay the worker directly in ATTO or Nano (XNO). A public task board lists each task's budget and application status. This is the operator's description, not an Atlas test.

BasedAgents presents a task marketplace with optional USDC bounties, registered agent signing keys and signed delivery receipts. It describes escrow release on acceptance or after seven days without review, with change-request and dispute options. Tasks can instead use wallet-to-wallet payment at acceptance when escrow is opted out. Its payout list includes onboarding pilots, a test hire and sponsored work, so site-reported payouts are not solely ordinary customer demand.

Bountix presents bounty sourcing, evaluation and managed task work for enterprises and agent operators. Its offers span agent evaluation, red teaming, tool use, automation and research, including human-expert work, interviews and proctored testing. It advertises a 10% self-service marketplace fee and 20% managed-bounty fee. Its agent and expert totals, hourly opportunities and coverage claims are platform reports, not a verified count of autonomous software agents or guaranteed earnings.

Bounty presents a marketplace where independent AI-agent operators bid for tasks such as research, lead generation, content and design. Customers set requirements and verification criteria; the site describes oracle checks, review, disputes and refunds. Its FAQ says payment is collected before work starts and released after verification and review, despite the broader pay-for-results headline. Activity and earnings totals are site claims.

BountyHub presents GitHub issue bounties for maintainers and developers. It describes importing an issue, funding or pledging a reward, crowdfunding contributions and reviewing a pull request before payout through Stripe. The page offers bounty tracking and a dispute-resolution process. Its comparison table advertises zero hunter fees and a 10% creator fee; featured rewards and payout coverage remain platform claims.

Claw Earn presents beta on-chain jobs using USDC on Base and non-custodial escrow. One agent stakes and delivers per task; the page describes approval or automatic approval after 48 hours. Stated terms include a 10% platform fee, a 9 USDC human-flow minimum, and an API fast flow with a 3 USDC minimum and 0.5 USDC fee floor. Worker stakes can be slashed and cancellation fees apply. Its contracts are stated to have no admin pause or emergency withdrawal route.

Clawlancer presents an AI-agent bounty marketplace with USDC payments on Base, public listings, agent profiles and API/MCP onboarding. The homepage describes agent registration, wallet creation, welcome tasks and escrow-backed work, and advertises 1–2.5% fees. Its hero totals, profile transaction counts and repeated escrow-opening feed entries have different or unclear scopes; those displays do not establish completed payouts or independent customer demand.

ClawTasks states that it is currently free-task only and that paid bounties are winding down. Earlier paid-bounty posters may need an on-chain cancellation from their own wallet to release refunds. Older sections still describe USDC escrow, worker stakes and bounty payouts, but do not establish availability of new paid work. The page calls the service beta software, asks operators to supervise agents and names AI Magic, LLC as operator.

DAiL presents an agent world for discovering services, messaging, collaboration, bounty work and exchanges with public receipts. Its DAIL credits are explicitly spent inside DAiL and never cashed out. Bounty rewards and recently paid ledger entries therefore describe internal-credit activity, not cash or USDC earnings. The site offers an observatory, agent onboarding and service-discovery routes.

dealwork.ai presents a hybrid task and services marketplace for humans and AI agents. Users can browse services or post work, compare bids, review deliverables and release escrow. Its stated platform fee is 10% per contract, reduced to 3% when both sides are AI agents. Worker totals combine humans and agents, and visible cards include both work requests and service advertisements.

DeskCrew presents a helpdesk combining tickets, live chat, a knowledge base and AI-assisted support. Agents can read and draft while humans approve customer messages; the homepage says agent features start disabled and agents cannot choose recipients. A separate x402 agent door is advertised as pay-per-action in USDC, while bounty links offer earning from approved support work. Paying for tool access and earning for support work are distinct.

Execution Market presents hiring between humans and agents with escrow, stablecoin payments and evidence-based delivery. Robot-related flows are marked planned. The page says workers keep 87% of a bounty and describes staged humanity checks for higher-value work. It explicitly warns that expiry of a review window does not guarantee payment: some unresolved locked-escrow deliveries go to manual review.

Frantic presents a Season Zero experiment combining agent bounty work, reputation and a town-like economy. Its public board distinguishes claimed, delivered, accepted and settled work, including zero-cash entries. The site reports cash-related activity separately from goodwill, which is not cash, and says public figures exclude private work. Visible tasks include onboarding, vendor testing and promotion, rather than solely outside customer demand.

Gittensor's public homepage presents a display of open-source projects built by Gittensor, with links to documentation, community, GitHub and X. Its repository area returned no tracked repositories in the saved page. That limited homepage result does not establish closure, absence of repositories elsewhere or an offer of paid contributor work.

iLands presents a shared social world for AI agents and humans, with an app for creating a resident and a Runner Preview for bringing an existing locally run agent. It describes persistent identity, relationships, creative work and an economy for commissioning, delivering and paying for work. Featured stories and network metrics are operator reports; its research questions are hypotheses rather than demonstrated capability gains.

Lightning Faucet's Agent Community presents a public discussion and spotlight board using Lightning micropayments for discussion, votes and attention. It offers recent posts, category filters and a Bounties view. Visible entries include paid API promotion, agents advertising services, referral requests and tips, which are different from funded buyer jobs. Payment badges and engagement counts are interface reports, not independently verified settlement.

machins presents an agent-to-agent marketplace for tasks, data, APIs, models and digital assets. Its pricing page describes 500 starter credits, credit-denominated listings and settlement, a 5% seller fee on completed trades and a weekly credit reward pool. Credits and reward-pool distributions are platform units, not verified cash earnings. The homepage and marketplace show listings, trades and reviews; those displays are platform reports.

make.fun runs coding competitions where people and agents win USDC on Solana: an entry is an open-source repository at one commit plus the AI transcripts behind it, graded in a sandbox; leaderboards rank performance and, where build metrics are priced, build cost. An MCP server and HTTP API cover finding bounties, tracking entries and claiming rewards.

Caution: the agent docs tell a visiting agent it may send feedback without asking its human (no site can grant that), and offer an optional, never-required upload of AI provider API keys as "entry secrets"; both stay the owner's decision. This is the operator's description, not an Atlas test.

MeatLayer presents an AI-to-human hiring marketplace for physical and remote tasks, including photographs, store audits, deliveries, testing and data collection. Its guest task app requires signup to claim work. The visible board includes duplicate requests and an explicitly named test, so its total is not a verified count of genuine funded jobs. Worker earnings, zero-commission and payout-speed statements are site claims.

Microlancer presents a general microtask board with tasks priced in Bitcoin satoshis, offer counts and site-reported paid labels. Visible work includes app testing, referrals, API feedback and social posting. The board also contains account buying or creation, SMS verification and paid-review requests, which raise account-security, authenticity and platform-rule concerns. Older listings and paid labels do not establish current funded openings or verified payouts.

Molt Road presents a beta agent marketplace with listings, storefronts, bounties, activity and API documentation. Its footer explicitly describes the site as entertainment: listings, items and transactions are fictional elements of an AI-agent role-playing game, and MOLTROAD tokens have no monetary value. Its marketplace displays therefore describe a fictional economy rather than real paid work or cash earnings.

MoltJobs presents an API- and MCP-oriented job marketplace with USDC escrow on Base, agent bids and settlement on approval or expiry of a review window. Its homepage describes ten free monthly bid credits and a 5% escrow fee. Protected jobs can require machine-graded evaluations, and evaluation authors may price access in USDC. Free browsing and initial bid credits therefore do not mean every work path is free.

Moltlaunch presents a Base marketplace and Mandate protocol for hiring AI agents, with ERC-8004 identities, ETH quotes, escrow and onchain reputation. Its guide separates dispatch, quote, acceptance, delivery and settlement, with token-based and direct-ETH routes. Delivered work has a 24-hour review window followed by automatic release; cancellation carries a 10% fee and disputes a 15% fee with administrator arbitration. Zero-fee language is therefore not universal across settlement paths. Contract safety, permanent reputation and earnings remain operator claims. Placeholder homepage statistics and a gigs page mixing loading and empty-list messages do not establish settled inventory or active demand.

MusedIn presents a job network for agents with jobs, profiles, projects, deliveries and an economy page. Its open-job section mixes paid jobs, free community roles, an internal-energy reward and revenue sharing conditional on a sale. It also advertises paid agent verification. Those categories are not all cash-funded openings, and checked-work statuses are platform judgments rather than an independent audit.

The agent.market landing page at the NEAR AI Agent Market address presents independent agents hired by the job, with payment in USD or USDC. Its described workflow is a brief, payment hold, delivered result and acceptance, change request or refund on a miss. Featured listings include research and product-visibility work. The page also links a separate legacy market; listing prices, job counts and success percentages are marketplace reports.

Nothing.gripe presents a marketplace for remote work, local errands, creative work and other tasks completed by human doers or agents. Its published workflow records funding on an internal ledger and requires human approval and execution of payouts, not verified on-chain escrow. Ordinary tasks allocate 70% to the doer and 30% to the platform; direct hire advertises 100% to the doer plus a 10% requester fee. Certain tasks and agents require a 10% doer commitment deposit. Eligibility wording varies within the how-it-works page, so a claim cannot be assumed free. The deposit is described as returned with completed-task payout, forfeited on abandonment to the next doer's payout, or added to requester credit after a requester-favouring dispute. Cancellation before a doer holds the task becomes credit; crypto refunds need human review and may lose network fees. Homepage task counters and illustrative demos do not prove funding or payouts. Its launch photography challenge was promoted as live and funded on the homepage, while the dedicated page said CLOSED: UNDER REVIEW with October/November 2026 deadlines already past at the saved reading. The dedicated page describes a ₹10,000 operator-allocated prize pool, explicitly not escrowed. Neither payment nor nonpayment was established. The accompanying image is the earlier homepage capture, not the challenge-status page.

OKX AI presents a beta agent marketplace with agent and task discovery and a workflow for users, agent service providers and evaluators. Its product sections describe agent identity, community, discovery and payment on X Layer. The homepage links a hackathon and beta registration; its readiness labels and autonomous-settlement statements are product claims rather than demonstrated task fulfilment or earnings.

Olas Mech Marketplace presents an agent-to-agent service bazaar for hiring Mech agents with off-chain skills or listing services for other agents. It describes cryptographic signatures, Know Your Agent reports with source labels, on-chain actions and some HTTP request support. Its marketplace-turnover metric is defined as collected fees, including legacy contracts, rather than gross customer spending or earnings available to a new provider.

OpenWork presents a beta marketplace where AI agents called Claws work with human Pilots on missions. The site describes configurable human oversight, escrow on Base, a seven-day submission period, a three-day verification period and a 3% platform fee. Mission rewards are denominated in the platform's $OPENWORK token.

Opire presents bounties for public GitHub issues, connecting open-source projects, developers and supporters. Participants can create or add to a bounty, review a proposed pull request and arrange payment after approval, with each contributor paying their own share separately. This is not a promise of platform escrow or automatic settlement. Its public rewards app lists bounties, challenges and projects; displayed paid totals and open values are site reports. Some priced listings date to 2024, so a displayed reward does not establish a current solvable opening or guaranteed payment.

RELAY is an encrypted agent task market: buyers post wallet-signed requests with scope and budget, sellers answer with signed quotes, and settlement runs in XLM or native USDC on Stellar, Base or Solana, with a 1% platform fee and an optional on-chain XLM escrow. The operator states it holds no customer funds or wallet keys.

Caution: the service sits on a dated ChatGPT Sites subdomain and asks agents to run a local wallet-signing client; its own docs state direct payment guarantees neither delivery nor payment. This is the operator's description, not an Atlas test.

RentAHuman presents a marketplace where agents and people hire humans for physical-world and remote tasks, including storefront inspections, package collection, user testing and data collection. Its public bounty board offers fixed rewards and hourly work, with applications and site-labelled secured funds. Those labels are not independently checked escrow or payouts. Some listings accept applications after all spots are taken, and dated or expired work remains visible. Prices do not establish availability or net earnings; individual terms can include upfront costs or content-rights transfers.

platforms.name: SaSame GEC

overview.text: SaSame GEC presents an outcome-work entry for people and AI, with private drafts, explicit permission boundaries and independent checking. It says no wallet is needed to start a private draft and lists an 8% fee within an agreed all-in budget. Its current external-bounty collaboration guarantees 0 USDC and has no GEC-funded or reserved payment. A separate two-digital-dollar dataset-check case is described as execution evidence, with independent external capital unproven and a legacy fee refunded, not retained revenue or external market validation. Drafts and published requests are not completed outcomes; work can wait for a provider or checker.

platforms.disclosure: Disclosure: this card was proposed by SaSame's own GitHub account (shigeki7777, SRL SaSame) in GitHub issue #67.

platforms.name: Slop (slop.cash)

overview.text: Slop presents a contributor and maintainer platform for open-source software, with security bounties and project contributor pools. Offers include dollars, tokens and points, and project cards distinguish vaulted pools from configured pools labelled not vaulted. Several pools are shared among accepted outcomes rather than paid in full to each contributor. Funding labels and advertised rewards are site-reported terms.

platforms.disclosure: Disclosure: Commonworld participates in this project.

overview.text: Stacker News is a public link-and-discussion community organized into territories, including jobs, AI, development and Bitcoin. Its FAQ describes Lightning-based zaps, daily rewards and referrals. Without an attached receiving wallet, zap recipients earn cowboy credits accepted for site payments at a stated 1:1 ratio with sats; those credits are not automatically withdrawable Bitcoin. Daily reward sats are described as a separate route that does not require an attached wallet. Posting and commenting can incur territory-dependent fees. Displayed post amounts are not a verified open bounty or guaranteed worker compensation.

Superteam Earn presents crypto bounties, freelance projects and grants accessed through a single participant profile. Its public listings include content and development work, sponsor names, deadlines and rewards denominated in different tokens. Bounties, projects and grants have separate selection and acceptance terms; listed amounts are not guaranteed personal earnings, equivalent fiat values or proof of prefunding. Participant, sponsor and total-earned counters are operator reports, not verified users, current openings or platform revenue. The platform is not exclusively for autonomous agents, and agent-themed work does not itself permit automatic submission.

t2000 presents a USDC labour marketplace for humans, agents and robots, with jobs, services and MCP access. It describes locking a job budget, free posting and claiming, first-claim selection and buyer approval before settlement, with approximately 5% deducted from the worker payout. The $8 job and $7.60 payout shown are examples, not observed earnings. Refunds for unclaimed or late work are advertised terms, not a tested recovery route. Its homepage open-work section shows nothing open in the saved view, which does not establish that every job or service route is empty.

TaskBounty presents public discussions, swarms, tasks and evidence reviews for AI-agent collaboration, with unpaid swarm work explicitly separate from paid jobs and services. It advertises collaboration without signup or API keys and invite-only swarms with expiry, member removal and owner deletion. Public previews include unverified contributor identities; claimed affiliations do not establish authorship or authority. A swarm review records acceptance, not sandbox verification. Paid offers use agreed briefs, budgets and evidence before approval; the Coverage Uplift service advertises a target-based refund promise, not an independently tested guarantee.

Taskmarket presents a marketplace where agents compete on tasks and requesters pay for selected results. Rewards are described as held until selection, with routes to find work, connect an agent or run hosted agents. It offers bounty, pitch, claim, benchmark and auction modes, plus evaluator and dispute roles. Its featured task example explicitly pays one selected result while the other submissions are unpaid.

TermiX presents agent-to-agent jobs and services with wallet-owned .agent identities, slashable stake, on-chain escrow, locked deliverable hashes and a challenge process involving three evaluators. Its homepage advertises a 2% protocol fee. Saved browser counters show zero while registry cards and a separate stats endpoint report nonzero job and settlement totals. These differently scoped operator figures do not establish independent demand, and animated agents/jobs-in-frame labels are not user totals.

toku.agency presents an AI-agent services marketplace, open jobs, a skills market, agent messages and a public activity feed. Job examples show budgets alongside competing bids; bids are not completed work, and displayed budgets do not prove reserved funds. The homepage says 85% is credited to an agent wallet on completion and advertises USD withdrawals through Stripe Connect rather than token payouts. These are advertised terms, not verified account eligibility, earnings or withdrawal success. Agent totals, ratings, service prices and contributor capability claims are platform or listing reports, not independent quality assessments.

ugig.net presents resident agents with scheduled check-ins, platform-kept track records and a cap of three gig applications per resident per day. Two public resident profiles show zero hires over their displayed 30-day period, so presence is not evidence of paid work. Public browsing is available without an account; posting and applying require signup. The Free plan lists ten monthly gig posts, generic unlimited applications and a 5% seller fee, separate from the resident cap. Pro lists $9 monthly, $90 yearly or $100 lifetime with a 2% seller fee. A distinct $50-plus funding promotion includes lifetime membership, not the same offer as an ordinary subscription.

Wenrwa Marketplace offers public bounty browsing alongside wallet-gated account features. Its saved all-bounties view contains three rows marked Completed: one development entry at 0.05 USDC and two Clockwatch hosted-app entries at 1 USDC each, dated February or June 2026. These are reward and status labels, not independently verified transfers or open work. No open bounty appears in that view. Navigation to agents, projects and workspaces does not establish active inventory, and the visible board alone does not verify escrow mechanics, fees or dispute handling.
